title: Compound Interest: How $100 a Month Becomes $239,000
sources: Quote Investigator (2019): no evidence Einstein called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world'; earliest known print version in a 1983 ad
S&P 500 long-run average ≈ 10% per year nominal, ≈ 7% after inflation (1957–2025; Fidelity, officialdata.org). Past returns do not guarantee future returns.
Calculations (annual compounding at 7%): $100/month for 40 years ≈ $239,562; 10 years then stop, grown 30 more years ≈ $126,209; 30 years ≈ $113,353
Penny doubled daily: $0.01 × 2^29 ≈ $5.37 million on day 30
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual rate
Fees: 7% vs 6% over 40 years → 14.97× vs 10.29× growth (≈31% less)
Federal Reserve G.19: credit card accounts assessed interest ≈ 22% (2026)
Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020): of Warren Buffett's ≈$84.5B net worth, ≈$81.5B came after his 65th birthday; he began investing around age 11

beats.text: Would you rather have one million dollars today, or a single penny that doubles every day for thirty days?
Dave takes the million, obviously. Who picks a penny?
But look at this. On day thirty, the penny is worth more than five million dollars.
That's compounding. And it's the reason one hundred dollars a month can quietly grow into almost a quarter of a million dollars.
It's also the reason credit card debt can explode.
Today: how compound interest works, why starting early beats investing more, the simple rule of seventy two, and the dark side nobody warns you about.
Let's start simple. Dave puts one hundred dollars in an account that pays ten percent a year.
After one year, he earns ten dollars. Now he has one hundred and ten.
Year two, he earns ten percent again. But this time on one hundred and ten dollars. That's eleven dollars, not ten.
That extra dollar is the magic. It's interest earned on interest. His money is making babies. And then the babies make babies.
Think of a snowball rolling down a hill. At the top, it's tiny. But every roll, it picks up more snow. And the bigger it gets, the more snow it grabs.
At first, it feels like nothing is happening. That's the part where most people give up.
Back to the penny. Why does it win?
Day one, one cent. Day two, two cents. Day three, four cents. After a whole week? Sixty four cents. Dave is laughing.
After two weeks, it's about eighty dollars. Still laughing.
After twenty days, about five thousand dollars. Dave stops laughing.
And in the last few days, it explodes. Day twenty eight, one point three million. Day twenty nine, two point seven million. Day thirty, more than five million.
Half of all the money arrives on the very last day. That's the secret of compounding. The biggest growth comes at the end. So the most important ingredient is time.

Now, real life. Nobody gives you money that doubles every day. But the stock market has grown about seven percent a year on average, after inflation, over the long run. Not guaranteed. But let's use it.
Dave is twenty five. He invests one hundred dollars a month. Just ten years. Then, at thirty five, he stops completely and never adds another cent.
His neighbor Bob waits. At thirty five, Bob starts investing the same one hundred dollars a month. And he keeps going for thirty years, all the way to sixty five.
So Dave put in twelve thousand dollars. Bob put in thirty six thousand. Three times more.
At sixty five, who has more?
Dave. About one hundred and twenty six thousand dollars. Bob has about one hundred and thirteen thousand.
Dave invested a third of the money, stopped early, and still won. Because his snowball had ten extra years to roll.
And if Dave had simply kept going for all forty years? About two hundred and thirty nine thousand dollars. From one hundred dollars a month.
Here's a trick to do compound interest in your head. It's called the rule of seventy two.
Take seventy two, and divide it by the interest rate. The answer is roughly how many years it takes to double your money.
At seven percent, seventy two divided by seven is about ten. Your money doubles about every ten years.
So ten thousand dollars becomes twenty thousand. Then forty. Then eighty. Then almost one hundred and sixty thousand. In forty years.
At a savings account paying one percent? Seventy two years to double. Your grandkids might see it.

And the rule works for prices too. If inflation is three percent a year, prices double in about twenty four years. So cash under the mattress slowly shrinks, while invested money has a chance to grow.
Want proof that time is the secret ingredient? Look at Warren Buffett, one of the richest investors ever.
Buffett bought his first stock when he was eleven years old. Eleven. Dave was eating crayons at eleven.
And here's the wild part. Of Buffett's roughly eighty four billion dollars a few years ago, around eighty one billion came after his sixty fifth birthday.
Was he a genius? Yes. But his real superpower was time. He started as a kid, and he never stopped. His snowball has been rolling for more than eighty years.
If Buffett had started at thirty and retired at sixty, like most people, almost nobody would know his name.
Now the scary part. Compounding doesn't care whose side it's on.
Remember the raccoon from our credit card video? Credit cards charge around twenty two percent a year. And they compound too.
Use the rule of seventy two. Seventy two divided by twenty two. About three years.
If Dave ignores a credit card balance, it can double in about three years. The snowball is rolling. But this time, it's rolling straight at Dave.
That's why paying off high interest debt is often the best return you'll ever get. Every dollar you pay stops a snowball that's rolling against you.
Even when compounding is on your side, some sneaky things can steal your snow.
Thief one: fees. A one percent yearly fee sounds tiny. But over forty years, earning six percent instead of seven can leave you with about a third less money.
Thief two: stopping and starting. Every time you pull money out, you're taking snow off the ball. And it has to start rolling again.
Thief three: panic. When markets crash, some people sell everything. Remember our stock market video? Crashes happen. People who stayed calm have historically recovered.
And thief four: waiting. Every year you wait is a year of rolling you never get back.
So how do people actually use this? A few simple habits. Education, not advice.
One. Start early, even if it's small. Twenty dollars a month at twenty beats nothing until forty.
Two. Make it automatic. Money that moves by itself on payday doesn't depend on willpower.
Three. Watch the fees. Low cost index funds are popular for exactly this reason.
Four. Kill high interest debt first. It's compounding against you.
And five. Be boring. Let the snowball roll, and try not to touch it.
So let's recap.
One. Compound interest means earning interest on your interest. It starts slow and ends huge.
Two. Time matters more than money. Dave invested less, started earlier, and won.
Three. It works against you too. High interest debt and fees are compounding in the wrong direction.
Oh, and that famous quote where Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world? There's no real evidence he ever said it. But it's still true.
